#6608. Girls Is Officially Returning for a Limited Run: Here’s What We Know

Fans have been pressing Lena Dunham to create fresh material for Girls for nearly a decade. On October 13, HBO confirmed that their wishes have finally been granted.

Amid the current reboot craze and a new generation of women finding the show, HBO has officially greenlit more episodes of Girls, with the core four cast members slated to return for a limited run. The news has been a long time in the making—in 2025, Dunham noted that she wasn’t opposed to bringing back Girls, should the right plot arrive.

“If we had something to say that was really specific and it was a moment in their lives where we felt like revisiting it—like millennial women becoming mothers or stepping into menopause or going to live at old-age homes—I would always want to work with those people again,” she told Variety at the time.

Following the arrival of the news, Amy Gravitt, the executive vice president, head of HBO & HBO Max Comedy Programming, shared, “We’re thrilled to have Lena turn her gaze from the tumult of one’s twenties to the milestone of turning 40. To say the world has changed since we last saw Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, Jessa, and Elijah is a massive understatement, but we know fans—old and new—will be happy to see how they’ve grown and relieved to see that they’re still the ‘Girls’ we knew way back when.”

Here’s what we know about the new Girls episodes.

Per HBO, the “returning cast will include Dunham as Hannah, Allison Williams as Marnie, Jemima Kirke as Jessa, Zosia Mamet as Shoshanna, Andrew Rannells as Elijah.”

Adam Driver has now confirmed that he won’t be returning for the Girls revival. When asked by CinemaBlend whether he would reprise his role as Adam Sackler, the actor gave a brief response: “No, but I wish them the best of luck.” Driver’s character was last seen in the series finale with Jessa (Kirke) after a failed attempt at getting back with Hannah (Dunham) to raise their baby together.

It’s currently unclear if Christopher Abbott, who starred as Charlie Dattolo, will reprise his role. Alex Karpovsky, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, and Jake Lacy also starred in the series, but we don’t know if they’ll return either.

In a press release announcing the news, Dunham said, “We always said we would only return to Girls if there was a specific story we were burning to tell. I’ve missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn’t quite picture them in the present day. Then, right around my fortieth birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking, it’s pretty hard to get them to stop… It’s rare that you get the chance to return to something that changed your life with the gift of hindsight and a whole new level of gratitude and understanding. I love these girls (and boy), our friends at HBO, and all the people who have continued to discover the show and remind us afresh why we do this, which is the joy of being together… and the chance to wear yellow mesh…”

During a November 12 event with Swarovski in New York, Dunham revealed that Williams was the first person that she asked to come back to the show, even before HBO had any idea that she wrote material for a reboot.

“It was starting to reach the moment where if we were going to revisit these characters, we really have something to say,” she told Williams in a sit-down conversation. “But you, before HBO, before anyone, you were my first call because it started with us and it ends with us.”

Dunham revealed that she was “nervous” about asking Williams back “because she’s a busy mom and producer and an iconic scream queen and she might not want to return to this,” but Williams joked that she would work with Dunham again even if it were to do an off-brand Gap ad.

That same day, Mamet also opened up about the lengthy process behind the revival. Speaking to Entertainment Tonight at the 2026 GQ Men of the Year red carpet, the actress revealed that discussions about bringing Girls back had been happening for quite some time before HBO officially moved forward with the project.

“I mean, it’s been in talks for a very long time,” she said. “But I kind of gave up because we’ve been talking about it for so long, and I don’t trust anything until I’m actually on set.”

Mamet added that once the official offer came through, things moved quickly. “Once they officially made an offer, it kind of came together pretty fast. So, I didn’t have to keep a secret for too long, which is good, because I’m not a good secret keeper.”

No plot details have been shared yet, but Dunham gave her thoughts on what each of the characters would be doing now in her 2025 Variety interview.

“Shoshanna was married to, then divorced from, the mayor of New York City, and she runs an athleisure startup that’s zero-waste. Marnie—it’s her third marriage. She still sings, but I think Marnie really needs to take it to Sex and Love Addicts Anonymous,” she mused. “Jessa is unvaccinated and lives on a boat in Croatia. Adam is a cult theater actor, and he’s probably living in Berlin, and Ray is still on city council and running his coffee shop and doing better than anyone. Elijah is the fourth lead on a sitcom, making a good amount of money and still looking for love in all the wrong places.”

When asked about Hannah Horvath, Dunham said that the character “teaches at Bard and loves raising her son. She probably has a girlfriend who’s, like, a chef. And she’s less obsessed with being famous. That is where I feel that she would land.”

The original show, which ran from 2012 to 2017, followed four millennial women in New York City struggling through their twenties and navigating relationships.

There is no release date for the new episodes of Girls, but HBO did confirm that “production is set to begin in 2027, 10 years after the season 6 finale.” The reboot will contain a total of five episodes.

#6607. Joe Budden Can't Stop Betting on Himself

This is an edition of the weekly newsletter Tap In, GQ senior associate editor Frazier Tharpe’s final word on the most heated online discourse about music, movies, and TV. Sign up here to get it free.

There’s Joe Budden, and then there’s everyone else. Despite the proliferation of rapper-led podcasts and talk shows in the last few years (itself a subset of the ever-ballooning celebrity podcast bubble), there’s no question who leads the pack—at least that’s how Budden sees it. It’s hard to argue with him: in February, Budden’s self-titled and pioneering podcast will turn 12,. Not too long ago, he posted a screenshot that “accidentally” revealed his yearly take-home was a number in the low eight figures.

Through it all, there've been dramatic cast changes, tense moments with rappers, hilarious must-see breakdowns of big moments in culture, and several dust-ups with Drake, a frequent subject of Budden and his co-host’s. Being part-New Jerseyian, I’m one of the vocal minority that believe it’s a travesty to reduce Budden’s rap career to “Pump It Up” (this is never far from my Recently Played to this day). Our paths actually crossed during his time at Complex, when I served as a sit-in for test episodes of Everyday Struggle while he searched for the co-host that would eventually become Akademiks—and even helped them launch the show with a series of digital short skits I wrote and produced that are probably lost to the internet by now.

As an occasional pod listener, I find it fascinating that Budden has defied all odds, and everyone who said he was bound to burn bridges, and now finds himself commanding attention, revenue and even reconciliations with his past employers. Despite how things went with State of the Culture, he’s back in business with Revolt. Joe Budden Network Presents, his new weekly series, premieres on November 13th, bringing his podcast to linear television through a unique micro-licensing partnership that allows Joe to retain full ownership of his IP.

To mark his next chapter, we talked about the current landscape of rap media and podcasting, the dangers of getting too comfortable, and how he plans to maintain his reign.

#6606. This Harvest Caesar Salad Is The Fall Side Everyone Asks Me To Bring

My love for Caesar salad knows no bounds, but in the fall, this harvest version is a STAPLE in my rotation. I first made it for a Friendsgiving last year, and people loved it so much that I ended up making it for my own Thanksgiving and Christmas celebrations, too. Every time, friends and family begged me for the recipe—it’s that good.

The best thing about it? It only requires a couple of easy ingredient upgrades to turn the classic salad into a fall favorite—here’s what makes it truly special.

As you’ve probably realized, this isn’t your plain Jane Caesar salad. There are two easy swaps that make this salad a side dish star. First, instead of romaine as the base, this salad lets kale shine. If you’re not a kale fan, stay with me. Once it’s massaged down with lemon juice and salt, it becomes perfectly tender and downright delicious—it’s the ideal hearty base for this salad.

The second and most important swap? Instead of sourdough croutons, this salad roasts pieces of butternut squash on a bed of freshly shredded Parm to create crispy frico squash “croutons.” As soon as I removed the tray from the oven and started breaking up the cheesy squash pieces, I had to remind myself that I couldn’t eat them all on their own—at least a few had to actually go in the salad.

This salad requires a few extra steps, but they’re quick and well worth it. First, make the Caesar dressing and refrigerate it until you’re ready to assemble. If you don’t have the time, a store-bought dressing will do just fine.

While that’s chilling, you’ll prepare the butternut squash croutons by cutting up your squash, shredding some Parm on an oiled baking sheet (don't use the pre-shredded kind—it just won’t melt the same), placing your squash on top, and baking until the cheese is crisp and browned on the bottom.

After you massage the kale with lemon and salt (don’t be stingy here—put those muscles to good use), all that’s left is to assemble! I highly recommend assembling in stages—dressing with the kale, then half the squash and Parmesan—before serving with the rest of the squash, Parmesan, and remaining dressing on the side for anyone who prefers more dressing than salad (again, guilty!).

#6605. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6604. Emma Watson’s Rare Appearance Came With a Vintage Valentino Look

Emma Watson may be keeping a low profile these days, but she hasn’t lost her eye for a good vintage find.

The actress stepped out on Thursday night at GQ’s Men of the Year party in Los Angeles, where she joined guests including Ayo Edebiri, Monica Barbaro, Tinashe, and more at the Chateau Marmont.

For the occasion, Watson wore a vintage patterned piece from Valentino’s collaboration with artist Christi Belcourt for its 2016 resort collection. She paired the colorful design with black-and-white striped Jacquemus stilettos for a lesson in pattern mixing and pairing.

The actress skipped the red carpet arrivals but was photographed outside the venue, staying relatively under the radar despite the star-studded guest list.

The outing marks another occasional appearance from the Harry Potter alum, who has largely stepped away from acting since completing work on Greta Gerwig’s Little Women in 2019. Earlier this month, she attended another Los Angeles event, the LACMA Art+Film Gala, in a sculpted ruby gown.

In a 2025 interview with Hollywood Authentic, Watson spoke about the decision to take a break from the industry, explaining that while she misses the creative process, she doesn’t miss the demands of promoting films.

“I do not miss selling things,” she said, describing that promotional side as “quite soul-destroying,” before adding that she does “very much miss using my skill set, and I very much miss the art.”

Watson has since explored other creative pursuits, including directing and her work on spirits brand Renais, which she co-founded with her brother, Alex. While she hasn’t announced a return to the screen, she has made it clear that she remains open to the right project and intent on being around people who share a passion for film.

“While I might not be making work right now, I still do feel that I’m part of a community,” she said in 2025. “I want to stay connected to that community and be part of it.”

#6603. I Want What Adorable New Moms Beanie Feldstein and Bonnie-Chance Roberts Have

Love is a many-splendored thing, especially when you’re gawking at it from the outside. In this column, we’ll be examining the celebrity couples who give us hope for our own romantic futures as we try to learn what we can from their well-documented bonds.

There was a period during what I like to call my “lesbian femcel era” (shortly after a breakup with the first woman I ever had real feelings for) when I had to mute any and all happy and in-love sapphic couples on social media in order to protect my own mental health. First up on my list? Beanie Feldstein and her wife Bonnie-Chance Roberts.

Luckily, I’m no longer down quite as bad as I used to be, which means I can enjoy Feldstein-Roberts updates—from their Gucci-clad 2023 wedding to the recent news that they’d welcomed their first child together—without undue jealousy.

Feldstein and Roberts met in 2018, during a Skype call to discuss the 2019 film How to Build a Girl, which Roberts produced and Feldstein ended up starring in. Feldstein came away from the meeting thinking Roberts’s name was Brooke, but at some point that must have been straightened out. “From the moment we first kissed, we both knew we would get married,” Feldstein told Vogue in 2023. Aw!

Three years later, Feldstein has shared with People that welcoming a daughter with Roberts “is the greatest gift. She’s such a good mom, and it’s so special to watch. Motherhood is unbelievably beautiful.”

The couple at the New York premiere of Focker-in-Law on Tuesday.

I can’t imagine how exhausting it is to do a press tour shortly after giving birth to your first child, but Feldstein was absolutely glowing while promoting Focker-in-Law at the film’s New York premiere this week—and Roberts was right by her side, looking extremely dapper in a bow-festooned white oxford that I absolutely crave.

I may not currently have a girlfriend (or a boyfriend or partner of any gender…this meme comes to mind), but some level of psychological health around other people’s joy has been achieved, because when I see Feldstein and Roberts out in the world together, all I feel is happiness that one of my favorite actors—whose delivery of “It is the titular role” in Lady Bird lives in my head rent-free—is so clearly, visibly in love. Mazel tov, cuties!

#6601. 10 Gnocchi Skillet Weeknight Dinners For Any Craving Or Time Of Year

All you need is one pan and less than an hour.

In our eyes, the hallmark of a great weeknight dinner is gnocchi. The comforting, pillowy pasta is the perfect vessel for endless sauces and flavor combinations, making it a star no matter the season or craving. Another bonus? In many of our favorite gnocchi dinners, there’s no need to cook the gnocchi beforehand. That means no waiting for water to boil or dirtying extra dishes. These 10 gnocchi skillet dinners bring all of your favorite flavors together in one pan, and all in under an hour. Simply put, gnocchi is made for weeknights.

A dirty martini happens to be the perfect template to turn into a savory recipe and we’ve riffed in many ways.? This dirty martini gnocchi is our latest attempt to transform the iconic drink into dinner, and we have to admit—it’s a success.

This is a true 30-minute meal, and it calls for ingredients that you might already have on hand. Like our other Marry Me dishes, this saucy one-pan dinner features a base of fresh garlic, sun-dried tomatoes, thyme, heavy cream, and Parmesan tossed with pillowy-soft and quick-cooking gnocchi, then topped with a pinch of red pepper flakes for a little extra spicy kick.

Creamy Pumpkin Gnocchi With Italian Sausage

For this creamy gnocchi dinner, we added pumpkin to create a comforting, nutty, and slightly sweet sauce that pairs perfectly with pillowy gnocchi and Italian sausage.

Out of all the party dips, spinach and artichoke reigns supreme in our book, so we turned it into this decadent pasta dish. We combined everything we love about our favorite dip—spinach, artichokes, cream & cheese—with quick-cooking gnocchi, turning it into an easy meatless dinner that’s loaded with flavor.

Every year, this chicken dinner is one of our most-loved recipes—it's not hard to see why. We paired chicken breasts with pillowy gnocchi in a creamy sauce, complete with mushrooms and spinach, all in one pan for easy cleanup.

In this new take on one of our most-popular dinners (creamy chicken & gnocchi), chicken breast cutlets are seasoned, pan-seared, then smothered in smoky, creamy spinach and mushroom sauce alongside plump gnocchi. It gets added flair from crumbled feta, ras el hanout, and spicy harissa paste—a North African hot sauce.

One of our most-popular dinners, this one-pan chicken bacon gnocchi is a weeknight favorite for very good reason. The creation of this dish all started with our one-pan chicken & gnocchi, which is so well-loved, we decided to upgrade it with one of our favorite ingredients: crispy bacon!

Let the good times roll because tonight’s dinner takes you down South to the cuisine of Louisiana with this chicken and pasta skillet. Just like our other gnocchi skillet dinners, this one is absolutely craveable; plus, it brings all the flavors we associate with New Orleans into your kitchen.

When developing this recipe, we took inspiration from the winning flavor profile of our Caprese chicken gnocchi soup, but anyone familiar with classic Caprese knows the basic formula: fresh mozzarella, tomatoes, basil, olive oil, and balsamic vinegar. In this recipe, We’re adding in pan-roasted chicken and store-bought gnocchi as Caprese’s newest co-stars.

Our one-pan creamy chicken and gnocchi is an all-time Delish favorite, but sometimes, you gotta try a few twists on a classic. Add Calabrian chile butter into the equation, and you might have just found your new favorite flavor combo.

#6600. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6599. Beyoncé Opens Up About How She and Jay-Z Kept Their Intimate Wedding Secret, Even From Guests

Nearly two decades after saying “I do,” Beyoncé is offering a rare glimpse into one of the most private moments of her relationship with Jay-Z. In a new interview with i-D, the singer reflected on their intimate 2008 wedding, revealing that the couple went to great lengths to keep the celebration under wraps.

“We had a very small wedding in our home,” Beyoncé told the publication. “We told the guests we were having a party, and no one knew they were coming to our wedding but our parents and a few friends.”

The couple hosted the ceremony at their New York City residence, and the date they chose (April 4) held special meaning for the pair, with the number four corresponding to both of their birthdays: Beyoncé was born on September 4, while Jay-Z celebrates his on December 4.

Beyoncé also discussed her wedding gown, which was designed by her mother, Tina Knowles. She called it her “favorite dress” that Knowles ever made for her in part because “it was gorgeously simple and made with her love.”

Her mom credited herself in a post celebrating the couple’s anniversary in 2020, saying, “ahem, I designed that dress.”

For the singer, choosing a design by her mother was never about making a fashion statement. “Wearing a dress she designed was very important to me, and more important than any designer dress,” she said.

#6598. Painter Sascha Braunig Pushes Through the Void

Sascha Braunig’s paintings have a tendency to produce visceral reactions: a pit in the stomach, an eyebrow raise, a need to move closer. This is not unintended.

“I want the viewer to have a bodily experience,” Braunig says.

The paintings are bright, smooth, candy-colored—lighthearted contrasts to the psychologically intense shapes: luminously rendered heads and torsos often bound by wiry tentacles. At times the figures recede into their matching optic backgrounds, as if hiding in plain sight.

Braunig, who is 43 and splits her time between New York and Maine, has been painting with this funky verve for close to two decades. Not long after she got her MFA from Yale’s painting program in 2008, she was having solo exhibitions of her small paintings of heads at the now-defunct Foxy Production in Manhattan. Inclusions at the New Museum Triennial and MoMA PS1 soon followed. (Attention from critics came quickly as well; one called her an “inspired reanimator of Surrealism,” another a “phenom.”)

Braunig is excellent at capturing the inherent tension of living in a body—especially one that is subjected to societal expectations of femininity. She’s playing with the ways women have been contorted and cinched and squeezed for time immemorial, asked to fit into archetypes that seem at turns glamorous or sinister. Often they are both.

“Our aesthetic, our personhood is formed in relation to these cultural forces and imagery,” she says. “You can’t separate yourself out from what you’ve seen throughout your whole life.”

These themes of gender performance and corporeal control permeate “Wrist Painter,” Braunig’s most extensive exhibition to date, which opens November 13 at the Portland Museum of Art. The show brings together some 45 works, including paintings, sculptures, works on paper, and sketchbooks. It will be her first solo institutional show in Maine. (A special occasion, as almost all of the pieces in the show were made a block and a half away, in her studio at the Portland arts nonprofit SPACE, over the last 15 years.)

“Sascha really stands out here in this arts ecosystem. She’s doing something really singular,” says Sayantan Mukhopadhyay, a curator at PMA who organized the show. When people think of Maine painters, they usually think of landscapes. But Braunig leans toward the cerebral, with a bit more bite. “The paradoxes are what really excite me about the work,” Mukhopadhyay says.

And the dichotomies are many. “Sascha has a way of presenting an abstraction that can read both soft and strong, feminine and violent,” says Olivia Smith, whose New York City gallery, Magenta Plains, now represents Braunig. “I think that’s what I’ve always loved: that she offers a way for the viewer to re-associate, which ends up telling them more about themselves than about Sascha.”

One of the earliest artworks in “Wrist Painter” is Sequins, from 2010. It’s from Braunig’s head series, which she began in grad school. Her process starts with a drawing, then she brings her sketch to life by making an embellished three-dimensional model. Then she’ll light the model and paint what she observes. She applies her lustrous oil paints with such precision that these strange bodily shapes start to look “real.”

She continued this system as she moved on to her bodies series a few years later, using clay resin, wire, and paper to make her maquettes. This haptic process is why works like Warm Leatherette, a 2015 painting at PMA that looks like a snatched Michelin Man encased in chartreuse padding, seem so tactile. (She has often described her choice of colors as “seasonal” or “dietary”—she finds a palette that works for one show and then cycles to a new one for the next.)

Her maquette process also lends a certain theatricality. She is literally setting up a scene, as if the entire idea of femininity were on a velvet-curtained stage, the whole specter aglow under klieg lights. What is gender if not a performance?

Braunig, who grew up in British Columbia, Canada, liked drawing and painting from a young age. Her father (a dentist) and mother (a nurse) enjoyed creative pursuits outside of work, and the house was full of art books. She loved watching Pee-wee’s Playhouse, which she credits as being just as formative, even more so, than going to museums.

Her parents encouraged her to attend an intensive summer art program at Skidmore College in upstate New York when she was 16. It was there that she first learned about Cooper Union, the New York City school where artists Lee Krasner and Wangechi Mutu got their start. Braunig decided it was the place for her.

New York City was the perfect place for the budding artist. “I was totally in love. It maybe ruined me forever,” she jokes now. She went to Yale right after Cooper, and then she moved to Maine in 2010, in her mid-20s. “I was really fortunate to have a New York gallery as I left the city, because I was able to have shows and have my work represented here even though I wasn’t here.”

Living somewhere far less expensive was also a game changer—she didn’t need to pile on jobs to make ends meet, and could instead focus on building her deeply personal style. “I had been exposed to so many influences coming to New York. And maybe those first five years in Maine were a time when I was able to process them alone.”

Braunig knows her art history, and she gets why people connect her style back to Surrealism. But her artistic comrades are more like French self-portraitist Claude Cahun or even Frida Kahlo, she says, “who’s really making work that is influenced by events of her own life.” Her art might feel dreamy (or perhaps like an acid trip), but “it’s not a dream space. I really am thinking about actual forces in the actual world.”

For many years Braunig used her work to illustrate broader ideas around culture and gender, but her most recent output has taken a turn toward the autobiographical. A few years ago she went through a creative block that left her stranded from her art practice, unable to make anything. As she emerged from this period last year, she started making her most personal paintings yet.

That work went into her radiant show “Cauldron” at Magenta Plains this past spring, its title a reference to the messy, transformative stew of midlife. Its anchor painting was My Death (2025), which, along with several others from the show, will travel to Portland for “Wrist Painter.”

Sascha Braunig, My Death, 2025, oil on linen over panel.

She calls My Death an “explicit self-portrait” about her own reanimation—an emergence through the void of creative block. It’s juicy and haunting and beautiful. She employed those tentacles again, but this time they are like a life force attached to a sleeping Braunig. A mysterious figure made from strips of vermilion orange pulls on them like marionette strings, bringing the artist back to life.

“I’ve come to understand that painting is a survival practice,” she says. “That can be a framing practice where you’re using it to talk about ideas in the world, or it can be a practice where you’re directly processing your own experiences. Maybe those two things aren’t that different.”

For the PMA show, Braunig has made one brand-new work, titled Torsion. At 78 inches tall by 60 inches wide, it is the largest painting of her career. She previously used the title for a museum show in Norway, but realized she’d never given it to an individual painting. The term, in physics, refers to the twisting of an object around an axis: a towel wrung out to dry.

This new Torsion is a painting of a fleshy pink figure with a tiny, twisted torso standing on tiptoes within a gray box. The figure’s muscular back is to the viewer, its knees fanning out in a plié. Dramatic tentacles in orange and yellow trace its exaggerated outline.

The figure’s head is cut off by the box’s ceiling, and its arms stop around the elbows, where they encounter the side walls. Maybe the figure’s been blocked, held back by the confines of this shadowy encasement. Or maybe, somehow, it has broken free.

“Sascha Braunig: Wrist Painter” is on view at the Portland Museum of Art in Maine from November 13, 2026, through March 14, 2027.

#6597. Ayo Edebiri Got the Forehead Curl Memo

Ayo Edebiri is one of the best-dressed people in Hollywood. In 2024, GQ named her a rising star in menswear. At our 2026 Men of the Year party, she made an even stronger case for herself as a style icon for the ages. Walking the red carpet at the Chateau Marmont in West Hollywood, the Emmy-winning actor continued her winning streak of power suiting in a navy chalk-stripe ensemble, a bright emerald-turquoise dress shirt, and a burgundy geometric tie. Her bob was styled in a side part, with a pronounced curl sweeping across her forehead. It’s a look that’s become a staple among Hollywood’s best-dressed men this year, a callback to Superman’s signature swoop, minus the Spandex tights and cape.

In the 1920s, the playful wisp of hair was known as the kiss curl: a deliberately placed lock of hair that sat on the forehead, even amid an otherwise carefully sculpted ’do. (As Seth Rogen helpfully pointed out on Instagram after we noted the kiss curl’s 2026 resurgence: “It’s called a Forelock.”) Its prominence in men’s grooming can be traced back in part to the French-American entertainer Josephine Baker, whose iconic curl ushered in an era—and now a century—of rogue forehead curls.

The kiss curl was so emblematic of the era that it made a triumphant return at the 2025 Met Gala, themed “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style.” A host of women paired the look with impeccable tailoring, including Simone Biles, Taraji P. Henson, Teyana Taylor, and, yes, Ayo Edebiri.

The modern appeal of the forehead curl is easy to understand. As hairstyles have grown longer, looser, and less structured, the curl lends an air of studied nonchalance—as if you didn’t spend too much time getting your hair just right. It’s sexy in a just-got-out-of-bed kind of way, especially when everything else—from the rest of the hair to the outfit—remains crisp, clean, and pristine.

As Edebiri once told Vogue of dressing for the red carpet: “One of the fun parts of getting to do this sort of thing is that you get to transform and be these different permutations of yourself.” At GQ’s Men of the Year party, she once again understood the assignment.

#6596. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6595. Inside the Y2K Costumes and Sets of Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson’s ‘Mouse’

The making of Mouse gave some Arkansas mothers a very good reason to have kept their daughters’ prom dresses. Costume designer Meg Grace put out a call on Facebook; in the week before the school-dance sequence was filmed, a member of her team drove around town collecting gowns, filling a van. Altogether, they gathered some 50 dresses worn to proms between 2000 and 2003. “It felt like a time warp,” Grace says of seeing them on the actors.

That flicker of recognition runs through the funny, affecting film from Ghostlight directors Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson. Set in 2002 in O’Sullivan’s hometown of North Little Rock, Arkansas, Mouse follows Minnie (Katherine Mallen Kupferer), a teenager accustomed to living in the shadow of her charismatic best friend, Callie (Chloe Coleman). After Callie’s sudden death, Minnie gravitates toward her friend’s poised mother, Helen (Sophie Okonedo), and the inviting home she has long preferred to her own. Their bond grows more complicated, shaped by affection, grief, and that familiar teenage longing to be someone else.

Mouse is particularly attuned to how a teenager’s dissatisfaction can attach itself to almost anything: imperfect skin, house clutter, a mother’s manner of speaking. The clothes and interiors do more than evoke an era; they reveal how Minnie sees herself and the life she wishes were hers.

O’Sullivan wanted the period embedded in her characters’ lives rather than presented as a cartoon version of the early 2000s. That required thinking about how trends actually reached teenagers there. “Arkansas wouldn’t be on the cutting edge of fashion in 2002,” she observes.

Grace, who grew up in Arkansas around the same time, recalls the stores available to her: JCPenney, Sears, Walmart, Big Lots, Kmart. “We might have all wanted to look like what we saw on TV, but what did you actually have access to?” she asks. You might wait until Christmas to ask for a shirt you’d coveted for six months. “That might be the one thing in your closet that’s really stylish, and then you make it work with everything else.”

For research, Grace consulted O’Sullivan’s yearbooks and pressed friends to unearth old photographs, including shots from their first digital cameras. “None of us knew how to put an outfit together,” she says, smiling. The challenge was to create looks that appeared as though a teenager had put them together with limited options and a still-developing sense of style.

Much of the wardrobe came from Arkansas estate sales and secondhand shops. Among the more discerning finds were the cargo capris, a once-ubiquitous garment largely overlooked by today’s Y2K revival. O’Sullivan recognized the look immediately: “With the polo—I was like, I wore this.” And the more dressed-up moments had their own awkwardness. Looking back at school dances, O’Sullivan remembers teenagers transformed by elaborate updos into “40-year-old princesses of a weird country.”

Production designer Linda Lee similarly sought to “create familiarity without creating a caricature.” That meant letting different eras coexist in the interiors. “The calendar might tell you that you’re in the 2000s, but your home doesn’t actually change that quickly,” she points out. Minnie’s house drew more heavily on the 1970s and ’80s, with bold colors and plenty of texture. Helen’s was more understated, incorporating elements from the ’80s and ’90s alongside newer additions.

The contrast extends beyond the decor. Minnie’s mother, Barbara (Tara Mallen, Mallen Kupferer’s real-life mother), is a single parent and veterinarian whose sympathy for hard-luck cases has filled the house with rescue animals. Her generosity leaves little room for domestic polish. Helen’s spacious home, with its freshly cooked dinners, offers Minnie an alluring alternative.

To dress the girls’ bedrooms, Lee cut up old issues of Seventeen and J-14 sourced on eBay, assembling the kind of wall collages teenagers made from what images they had at hand. There were other bedroom essentials to track down too: O’Sullivan remembers Lee announcing, “We have secured the lava lamp.”

The film’s 2002 setting also shapes its portrayal of grief. “I don’t know how to write teenagers now, quite honestly,” O’Sullivan admits. “The way that we grieve has changed so much, culturally, with social media.” The story draws on her own experience of losing a friend in a car accident at the end of her junior year in 2001, though Minnie’s relationship with Helen is fictional.

In the film’s largely offline world, news arrives not immediately and simultaneously but at its own pace, while public, sometimes competitive displays of grief require taking action rather than simply posting a photo carousel. Cell phones are present but hardly universal: A Sidekick makes an appearance, and Callie has a chunky Nokia. (“Indestructible phones,” Lee calls them. “Could play Snake for hours,” O’Sullivan adds.)

For today’s teenage viewers, however, even the film’s most ordinary details can come as a surprise. After seeing Mouse, a young neighbor asked O’Sullivan, “Wait, your mom could pick up another phone in the house and hear your conversation?” She assured him that this was indeed possible—“and,” she says, shaking her head, “the source of a lot of stress.”

#6594. The Voice Behind The Pillsbury Doughboy’s Iconic Giggle Has Passed Away

A little giggle that left a big impression.

JoBe Cerny, the actor who gave the Pillsbury Doughboy his signature voice and unmistakable giggle, has died at age 78.

According to TMZ, Cerny died on October 30 in Illinois following a years-long battle with Alzheimer’s disease. His son, Tim Cerny, confirms the news to the outlet, explaining that his father was diagnosed around 2020 and eventually stepped away from the beloved role as his health declined.

For anyone who grew up watching Pillsbury commercials, Cerny’s voice is probably a lot more familiar than his face. He voiced the Pillsbury Doughboy, also known as Poppin’ Fresh, from 2014 until around 2020, bringing the cheerful baking mascot to life with the giggle that generations of viewers have come to recognize and adore.

Cerny took over the role, previously voiced by both Paul Frees and Jeff Bergman, becoming part of the character’s decades-long history in American advertising.

Following the news of his death, fans have been sharing memories of the Pillsbury Doughboy and the small moments of happiness Cerny’s work brought them.

“Nooo! Ugh I loved his voice would cheer me up when I was having a crap of a day!” one Instagram commenter wrote.

Another shared a particularly nostalgic reaction: “I loved the doughboy as a kid! Didn’t know he voiced him!”

Others reflected on how much the commercials meant to them growing up. “Childhood leaving us day by day. Back then commercials were actually good,” one person commented.

And one fan even has a special tribute planned: “Will be buying the rolls tonight in his honor 🙏🏻,” they wrote.

The reactions remind us how recognizable the Pillsbury Doughboy became over the years. Even if viewers didn’t know Cerny by name, they knew the character and the familiar laugh he helped bring into their homes.

In addition to his voice work as the iconic Doughboy, Cerny also did commercials for Cheer laundry detergent and made appearances in movies including My Best Friend’s Wedding and Legally Blonde 2.

Outside of his entertainment career, Cerny was an enthusiastic model train collector and racing fan who continued driving go-karts into his 60s, according to his obituary.

Although Cerny spent decades working in entertainment, his time as the voice of one of America’s most recognizable food mascots remains an especially memorable part of his career.

And judging by fans' reactions, that little giggle made a much bigger impression than he might have realized.

#6593. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6592. Andrew Garfield’s Hair Is the Mane Attraction

Andrew Garfield’s hair is very long—and oh so glorious. When the 43-year-old actor sat down with GQ for his 2026 Men of the Year interview, he told us he’d grown his current shoulder-length mane for his role as Roy Horn (of Siegfried & Roy tiger-wrangling fame) in the upcoming series Wild Things. Production ultimately put him in a wig, but Garfield kept the length regardless. And thank goodness he did. The actor brought his enviable mane to the red carpet at our annual Men of the Year party at the Chateau Marmont in Los Angeles on Thursday night, where it held its own among Hollywood’s finest.

The Artificial star arrived in an Edward Sexton suit, accessorized with a Breguet watch. But, as has been the case lately, his hair was the real headliner. The neck-grazing length was in fine form, with a few stray strands tucked neatly behind his ears. And then there was the forehead curl: a particularly on-trend flourish that’s found its place atop some of this year’s best-dressed stars (including Ayo Edebiri).

We first caught a glimpse of Garfield’s longer locks at Wimbledon this summer in London. At the time, his longtime hairstylist, Lucy Halperin, let us in on the secret to the look: a little sea salt spray, styling cream, and a diffuser to bring out his natural curls and waves. The combination enhances the hair’s volume while keeping frizz at bay.

That said, Halperin also credits his good hair to a bit of genetic luck. “Sometimes we just give it a good little wet down, and it kind of just works with him,” she told us at the time.

Whatever transformations Garfield has in store for his next on-screen role, we hope this particular look sticks around. Because if Thursday night was any indication, he’s not quite ready to part with it—and frankly, neither are we.

#6590. Dakota Johnson and Machine Gun Kelly’s Full Relationship Timeline

Dakota Johnson and Machine Gun Kelly have yet to define their relationship publicly, but the two stars have been spending plenty of time together.

The actress and musician were first linked in September 2026, when they were photographed together in New York City. Days later, a source told People that Johnson and Kelly, whose real name is Colson Baker, “have been hanging out and seeing each other under the radar for months now.”

The two stars had known each other before, but according to the source, they became closer after attending Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding in July.

Since then, Johnson has watched Kelly walk the runway in Milan, and sources have shared more about how their connection developed.

Below, everything we know about Johnson and Kelly’s rumored relationship so far.

Johnson and Kelly both attended Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s July 3 wedding at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

The two stars already knew each other, but a source close to Kelly told People in September that they “hit it off” at the wedding.

On September 28, a source gave Entertainment Tonight similar intel, telling the outlet that Johnson and Kelly “really connected at Taylor and Travis’s wedding.”

On September 12, Johnson and Kelly were photographed together in New York City, getting out of the same SUV and entering Swift’s Tribeca apartment.

Four days later, a source close to Kelly told People that Kelly and Johnson “have been hanging out and seeing each other under the radar for months now.”

The source explained that Johnson and Kelly “started off as friends and were texting often, but now they’re spending more time together.”

“It’s a very new start, but they’re smitten with each other right now,” the insider added. “They haven’t put a label on their relationship yet. They are just seeing where spending time together will take them.”

A second source characterized things as “super casual” at that point.

On September 22, Johnson and Kelly both traveled to Italy for Milan Fashion Week and attended the same event.

Three days later, Johnson addressed the broader attention her dating life receives during an appearance on Vogue’s The Run-Through podcast, though she never mentioned Kelly specifically.

“Even if I go to dinner with my manager or my lawyer, it’s like, ‘Seen with mystery man,’” she said. “I also don’t care.”

When asked whether she ever feels compelled to correct speculation about her personal life, Johnson explained why she prefers not to engage with it.

“I think it’s just futile. People are gonna believe what they wanna believe, and I don’t have the energy to fight for that,” she said. “I would much rather focus on other things in my life. Every day, there’s something on the internet that’s ridiculous and true or not true, and I don’t care.”

On September 28, a source shared more about Kelly and Johnson’s relationship with Entertainment Tonight: “Dakota was the one who made the first move. He’s very shy around her, but he likes her a lot. It’s still new, but they’re having fun and seeing where things go.”

The insider added, “Dakota has been a fan of his music and has always found him cute. He likes her a lot, too.”

On October 19, a source close to Kelly told People that he and Johnson were spending more time together. “They have been out on dates that people don’t know about because there aren’t any photos.”

The insider said that they’re in the “dating phase,” and “aren’t ready to go official yet.”

“They both really like each other and have been seeing each other more frequently,” the source shared. “They haven’t put a label on their relationship yet, but they’re growing closer every time they hang out.”

In the past few months, they’ve especially connected over their “same dry and dark sense of humor,” the source said. “[They] make each other laugh.”

Days later, Kelly and Johnson were photographed out in Los Angeles on October 23. They first left a music studio together, riding off in Kelly’s red Maserati. That evening, they were seen together again, leaving the Chateau Marmont.

A source close to Johnson gave People an update on their dynamic on October 28. “She’s happy and enjoys spending time with him,” the insider said. “There’s a lot of chemistry and she’s been going to the studio with him while he works. For now, it makes her happy.”

On November 3, Kelly and Johnson were photographed leaving a restaurant in Calabasas, California, after a dinner date. They were smiling and talking to each other in the shots.

Two days later, on November 5, Johnson and Kelly stepped out for another evening together in Los Angeles, attending a Khaite dinner at Dan Tana’s in West Hollywood. For the occasion, Johnson wore a black Death Row Pictures zip-up hoodie over a lace-trimmed Valentino miniskirt, paired with knee-high Gucci boots and statement diamond jewelry. Kelly opted for a more casual look, wearing a green satin bomber jacket over a yellow hoodie and gray sweatpants.

The next week, Johnson and Kelly stepped out for another evening together in Los Angeles on November 11. The pair first attended a screening of Johnson’s short film Flesh Impact, before heading to dinner at the Tower Bar inside the Sunset Tower Hotel with friends. #6588. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

Both ensembles sure were bright, but ask any color theorist and they’ll probably tell you that wearing green on a red carpet is a surefire way to stand out—they’re opposite of each other on the color wheel for a reason!

If the MOTY red carpet can provide any insights into the year of fashion ahead, we’ll surely be seeing even more green in the months to come. We’re manifesting abundance, in more ways than one.

#6584. One-Pan Creamy Spinach-Artichoke Gnocchi

Out of all the party dips, spinach and artichoke reigns supreme in our book. While we’re all for a chip-and-dip dinner, that’s not the most family-friendly weeknight meal, so we turned it into this decadent pasta dish. We combined everything we love about our favorite dip—spinach, artichokes, cream & cheese—with quick-cooking gnocchi, turning it into an easy meatless dinner that’s loaded with flavor. It’s easy enough for when you’re just craving comfort food (just one pan!), but fancy enough to serve to guests too.

Top tips & variations:We added briny capers here to help cut through all the richness, but if you’re not a fan, feel free to skip. While the gnocchi simmer, stir to prevent sticking, and try to keep them in an even layer so they stay submerged and cook evenly. The recipe calls for marinated artichokes because they’re already flavored with ingredients like garlic and red pepper, but canned or frozen will work in a pinch too.

It’s up to you if you’d like to only bake it until melted or take it one step further by letting your gnocchi sit under the broiler for a minute to get some attractive browned spots. Whichever you choose, we definitely recommend the final basil garnish to add flavor and freshness to your final dish.

Storage:Have leftovers? Store them in an airtight container in the fridge for 3-4 days.

#6583. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6581. Florence Pugh Sees Your Statement Coat and Raises You a Statement Shoulder

Forget the statement coat. Florence Pugh is all-in on the statement shoulder. And, in true Florence Pugh fashion, she’s doing nothing by halves. At an East of Eden FYC event in Los Angeles, the actor arrived wearing a black satin Harris Reed ensemble with shoulders of such exaggerated proportions that they practically deserved their own invitation.

Styled by Rebecca Corbin-Murray, Pugh wore a look from Reed’s spring 2027 collection, featuring enormous, sculptural sleeves that rose above her head like a pair of black wings. Beneath all that architectural drama was a tightly fitted, button-front corseted jacket and a slim pencil skirt, a silhouette that balanced Victorian severity with something subversive. (The look actually first appeared in the bridal-focused collection in all-white, but Pugh and Reed decided on the more gothic vibe.) She added towering Vivienne Westwood platform sandals and a constellation of diamond earrings from Maria Tash.

It’s hardly surprising that Pugh would turn to Harris Reed for such a theatrical yet elegant moment. The British designer is a longtime friend and collaborator: Pugh opened his fall 2023 London Fashion Week show in a sequined harlequin gown and enormous halo headpiece, delivering a Shakespeare-inspired monologue about the transformative power of clothes. She returned to open his fall 2025 presentation at Tate Britain, emerging in a pointed black corset and hooded gown for an eerie, dramatic performance. Reed’s designs, with such unabashed romanticism and allegiance to craft, have long been a natural extension of Pugh’s own fashion sensibilities.

The beauty look was equally striking. Makeup artist Alex Babsky gave Pugh a deep, wine-stained lip, softly smoked mauve-gray eyes, and flushed cheeks, while hairstylist Adir Abergel twisted her blonde hair into a deliberately undone, almost Regency-style updo, with wisps escaping around her face.

The night before, Pugh had embraced a more relaxed take on historical dressing. She appeared alongside her East of Eden co-star Zoe Kazan in a richly patterned Ralph Lauren Collection jacquard Maurice jacket, layered over the matching Thurlow corset top and a dark, floor-length Janie maxi skirt. She added Bulgari Serpenti Viper jewelry, Maria Tash diamond earrings, and chunky Christian Louboutin platform sandals to keep things modern.

Throughout the East of Eden promotional circuit, Pugh and Corbin-Murray have found a particularly satisfying meeting point between the actor’s maximalist instincts and the romantic, historical world of the Netflix adaptation. There have been enormous black Rodarte ruffles, a corseted Vivienne Westwood gown in shocking chartreuse, and an Erdem ensemble that paired sparkling lingerie with a kilt—the prettiest looks always come with a rebellious streak. While this time the finishing touch was the XXL shoulders, she recently made her red carpet debut with boyfriend Finn Cole on her arm.

Corsetry has emerged as a common thread, but Florence Pugh has never been one to play the demure period heroine. The bigger the shoulders, the better.

#6578. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.
